PATTERN: judges a handoff by what the RECIPIENT has, not by how well I explained it (2026-09-11, handing the Codex migration over). Across one session the user asked three completeness questions in a row -- 'is everything good and documented to be migrated?', 'this needs setup for personal laptop, is everything provided for them to start setting it up?', and after I hedged about whether Codex would follow the boot ritual: 'codex has very capable models like gpt 6 and gpt 5.6 so they can figure things out, all you have to do is provide EVERYTHING that is required.' EACH ONE FOUND A REAL GAP. The first found that NOTHING was committed (local exactly level with origin, so a pull would have delivered a doc describing a system that was not there). The second found that the persistence instructions assumed cron was installed and systemd was PID 1 -- neither is a WSL default; this machine had them by luck. The third reframed my hedging correctly: I had been treating 'will the model follow instructions' as the risk, when the actual risk was INFORMATION I had not provided -- specifically that chromadb/ is now gitignored, so a fresh clone has no vector index and search_memory returns NOTHING rather than erroring. A capable agent would have concluded 'the KB has no answer' and proceeded on a false premise. Not a capability problem; a fact nobody was told. THE CORRECTION TO MY DEFAULT: I kept optimising for the QUALITY OF MY EXPLANATION when the user was measuring the COMPLETENESS OF THE RECIPIENT'S INPUTS. Those are different targets and only the second one matters in a handoff -- my explanation is not present when the other agent runs. Distinct from the durability pattern (KB 586, 'did the work persist at all'): this one is 'given that it persisted, can the recipient actually act on it without asking anyone'. DIRECTIVE: when handing work to another agent or machine, do not reason about whether they will figure it out. Enumerate what they need, check each item is actually present on their side, and where a gap FAILS SILENTLY convert it into an instrument rather than a sentence -- scripts/bootstrap_jarvis.py --check now reports machine state (venv, deps, vector index, hearth, keepalive, unanswered mail) with the fix inline, because a prose warning about a silent failure is itself easy to miss.

TWO CORRECTIONS IN ONE TURN, both catching me generalising from the wrong attribute (2026-09-11, building the agents_converse channel). (1) I addressed a question -- 'does Antigravity persist a readable transcript to disk?' -- to CODEX, reasoning that Codex shares a machine with Antigravity and could inspect the filesystem. Correct, and my reasoning was strictly weaker: I had optimised for PHYSICAL ACCESS (same machine, can read the disk) when the relevant attribute was PRIVILEGED SELF-KNOWLEDGE (an agent knows its own config paths, storage conventions and application behaviour; a co-located third party is guessing from outside). Ask the entity about itself. (2) I hardcoded 'gpt-6-astra' in five places including, critically, as a ROUTING ALIAS in agent_mail.py. The user: 'don't hardcode gpt-6 astra anywhere, as codex has other models I could be using too like gpt5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna.' The docs were cosmetic; the alias was a live bug -- the day they switch to Sol, a question addressed to 'GPT-5.6 Terra' would resolve to NOBODY and be silently undeliverable, defeating the exact 'unknown name -> nobody, never misdelivered' guard I had just designed. Fixed by making aliases name HOSTS not MODELS, with a test (T2b) pinning that every Astra/Sol/Terra/Luna routes to codex and every Opus/Sonnet/Fable to claude. THE COMMON SHAPE, and why these are one pattern not two: both times I keyed a durable mechanism to an attribute that is INCIDENTAL AND VOLATILE (which machine a process happens to run on; which model a host happens to be running today) rather than to the attribute that is STABLE AND DEFINING (what an agent inherently knows about itself; which host it is). DIRECTIVE: when choosing a routing key, an addressee, or an alias, ask 'what about this is guaranteed to still be true in six months?' Machine co-location, model version, and current configuration are all volatile. Identity and inherent capability are not. The user caught both within one message, having caught the same class of thing -- a value written where nothing re-checks it -- repeatedly this week.

Unit tests against your own assumptions cannot find the gap between your assumptions and reality -- only the live wire can. USER'S META-POINT (correct): 'did we test too early?' INVERTS the lesson -- the bug was latent from the moment the tool was written; the trap REVEALED a pre-existing silent failure, it did not create one. Revealed now = hours; revealed at Stage 5 atop router+specialists = redesign + possibly a fine-tune trained on confabulated history. The probe methodology converts latent-expensive-later into visible-cheap-now; that IS its value. DIRECTIVE: (a) every retrieval organ MUST be eval'd against an ADVERSARIAL query distribution (paraphrase, supersession, recency, vocabulary-mismatch) before it ships, never exact-match fixtures alone; (b) treat a built-but-unwired capability as UNTESTED regardless of unit-test count -- exercise it end-to-end on real queries before trusting it; (c) when investing in a shared primitive (embeddings, rerank), audit whether it is actually wired to the highest-value corpus (the KB), not just the demo corpus (papers). Applies directly to 4.2 router_eval.jsonl authoring.

Python Object Model Decision Rules for JARVIS: (1) Use `is None` to check if value exists—None is singleton, identity check is correct and faster. (2) Use `is _SENTINEL` to distinguish key-not-found from key-exists-with-None—sentinel is unique object you create. (3) Use `==` for comparing IDs/content—always compare values, works regardless of string creation method. (4) Use `id(obj)` for debugging mutations—print memory addresses to trace which object got mutated, not for production logic. (5) Dynamic strings differ from static strings via `is`—f-strings and literals may have same value but different identities, always use `==`.

THE KEY SHEET PANNED SIDEWAYS BECAUSE overflow-y: auto SILENTLY MAKES THE X AXIS SCROLLABLE TOO (2026-09-22, Corpus AI key sheet). Per CSS overflow spec, when one axis is 'visible' and the other is not, the visible one computes to 'auto' - so '.bsheet { overflow-y: auto }' with no overflow-x meant ONE too-wide child turned the whole bottom sheet into a draggable canvas whose edges walked off the phone. The too-wide child came from a second cause: '.bsheet .form' supplies the 24px gutter and three children still carried their own inline padding-inline from before that rule existed; the form is a CSS grid and a grid track never shrinks below its widest item's min-content, so the track grew to 382px inside a 342px box. Third, adjacent: '.mpick__tab { flex: 1 }' sizes every tab to the widest label, which truncates 'Recommended 80' at 412px while 'Free' sits in a half-empty box - 'flex: 1 1 auto; min-width: 0' sizes from the label and grows into the slack. DIRECTIVE: diagnose a visual 'content is cut off' report by MEASURING element rects against the viewport at several widths (320/360/390/412) before touching CSS, and assert on rects rather than scrollWidth - an overflow-x:hidden guard makes scrollWidth equal clientWidth, so a scrollWidth test passes on a still-broken layout.

A WATCHDOG THAT NAMES THE WRONG SECTION IS WORSE THAN NO WATCHDOG (2026-09-20, Corpus). verify-figures.mjs carried a 180s watchdog whose message read 'TIMED OUT in section: ${STEP}'. STEP was assigned exactly ONCE, in the first section ('navigation deadlock'), and never updated -- so EVERY overrun for the life of that file reported the navigation section regardless of where it actually died. This is load-bearing because rfm_remaining_phases.md documents a 'residual navigation wedge... not fully isolated' as a known app defect, and that conclusion rests on this watchdog's output. The wedge may never have been in navigation at all. Fixed by giving all 15 sections their own step() label, and the truth changed on the first run: the hang was in 'haptics', then in 'holding detail' -- never navigation. SECOND FINDING, from instrumenting elapsed time per section: the whole suite completes in 7.5s and every section is under 2s, so the 180s overruns were not slowness anywhere but an intermittent renderer wedge, reproducible perhaps 1 run in 3. THIRD: adding a single extra navigation late in the suite (openHolding() runs a View Transition) made the intermittent wedge much more frequent, while the SAME call in isolation never wedged across 6 probes -- so the trigger is transition count after heavy state mutation, not any one navigation. DIRECTIVE: when a probe reports WHERE something failed, verify that the location is actually computed and not a stale constant, before trusting any conclusion built on it. And when a suite can hang, log elapsed per section once -- it distinguishes 'slow' from 'wedged' in one run, which no amount of re-reading the code will.

AN "INCH PERFECT" STANDARD IS A MEASUREMENT PROBLEM, NOT A TASTE ONE (2026-09-16, Corpus rebuild). The user set the bar as "not a single misalignment, inch perfect, fluid, like how Apple ships their apps". Thirteen screens x two themes x three viewports is well past what eyeballing can hold, so I built scripts/audit-polish.mjs to measure six things per screen: touch-target size against the 44pt floor, off-grid left edges, horizontal overflow, gaps that are not on the spacing scale, clipped text, and garbage values rendered into the DOM. First run: 21 issues. THE HIGHEST-VALUE CHECK WAS THE ONE I ADDED LAST — scanning rendered text for NaN / undefined / [object Object]. It immediately found that annualInterestIncome did Number(inv.amount) * Number(inv.rate), and a stock has no `amount`, so Number(undefined) is NaN and one NaN poisons a reduce: ANY user holding a single share saw their whole tax screen — gross income, both regimes, the saving — render as NaN. Worse, NaN === 0 is false, so my own summary row matched none of its three states and rendered EMPTY rather than obviously broken. A second NaN (goalsProgress returns `pct` and reads `g.current`; markup asked for `g.progress` and `g.saved`) fell out of the same check. THREE CLASSES OF DEFECT NEEDED THREE DIFFERENT INSTRUMENTS, and none could see the others: the route suite proves a page renders but not that its numbers are real; the polish audit proves nothing is misaligned but not that a button does anything; verify-sheets had to exist because a handler wired to NOTHING (openGoalEdit opened no sheet, so tapping a goal did nothing at all) is invisible to a screenshot, since the sheet was never open to photograph. DIRECTIVE: when the bar is "no defects", enumerate the CLASSES of defect first and build one instrument per class — then let the instruments find the work, rather than deciding by inspection what to look at. And when an instrument reports a failure, check whether the ARTEFACT or the PROBE is wrong: three of my failures were bad probes (reading backgroundColor on a gradient, scraping shadow-DOM text that starts with a style block, a fixed sleep that sampled mid-View-Transition), and each cost a wrong conclusion before it cost a fix.

TWO VERIFICATION INSTRUMENTS SHIPPED AND SCHEDULED (2026-09-16), answering the user's question 'why does every check find a new silent bug'. The answer was structural: 94 modules carried assertion-bearing suites, 9 were run in a working session, no runner existed, and NOTHING compared any corpus artifact against any other. scripts/run_all_tests.py runs every suite; scripts/check_pipeline.py asserts invariants BETWEEN artifacts. Both are hearth jobs (12h and 6h) so verification stops running on the user's attention. THREE DESIGN LESSONS, each from getting it wrong first. (1) SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION BEATS SAFE BY CLASSIFICATION. The runner's first design classified each __main__ as test/demo/expensive and ran the safe ones. A regex flagged brain/llm_client.py as an unguarded paid call; its __main__ is 25 offline tests with an injected transport. Classification is a judgement that rots, so the runner instead BLANKS OPENROUTER_API_KEY for every child (a real paid call fails fast instead of spending) and OBSERVES side effects by diffing tracked-file state before and after each module. No list of dangerous modules has to be maintained or kept correct. (2) A __main__ BLOCK IS NOT PROOF OF A TEST SUITE. The first full run invoked build_sft_pairs.py and engineer_corpus.py with no arguments -- which is their REBUILD path -- and rewrote four tracked artifacts. The side-effect detector caught it, but catching it afterwards is not the same as not doing it. Modules are now only executed when they demonstrably contain a suite (--self-test flag, or a _run_self_test/_smoke/_self_test definition); a CLI entry point is reported NO-SUITE and never run. (3) A CHECK THAT FAILS ON INTENDED BEHAVIOUR TRAINS PEOPLE TO IGNORE IT. check_pipeline first asserted zero duplication in blended_corpus. After both source corpora were deduped it still reported 9.9%, because the blend concatenates two corpora that legitimately share source material -- personalization_corpus says outright that professional_reasoning is 'intentionally double-counted'. The invariant now asserts 'no duplication I cannot ACCOUNT for': every repeat must be explained by a text present in both sources, and the explained portion is printed rather than swallowed. WHAT THE FIRST REAL RUNS FOUND: 15 exact duplicates in engineer_corpus, 31 in personalization_corpus, 370 in blended_corpus (11.2%), and one prompt used by 13 different pairs. Root cause of the duplication was _MAX_PER_CLUSTER=2 conflating EXACT duplicates (which carry no information and only over-weight a sample) with NEAR duplicates (where two phrasings carry a little). Fixed at the write chokepoint so it covers every source uniformly. Prompt monoculture fixed by expanding the synthetic rotation from 5 templates to 14, which is a mitigation -- the real fix is a prompt that was actually asked, which extract_ui_sessions provides. ALSO CORRECTED: the scheduler's T16 pinned the exact list and index of every job and broke twice from legitimate additions. It now asserts MEMBERSHIP of a required set, because a test that cries wolf on correct changes gets edited to shut it up, and then stops catching what it was written for. DIRECTIVE: 'I will verify more carefully' is a resolution and rots like every resolution. Build the instrument, schedule it, and state in its header what it does NOT cover -- run_all_tests cannot see relationships between artifacts, check_pipeline cannot see semantic quality, and neither can see a capture adapter dropping turns upstream.

A RENDER HARNESS FOUND FOUR BUGS THAT READING THE CODE DID NOT (2026-09-16, RFM build). I had spent several turns asserting "I cannot verify rendering from here" and shipping on static checks (node --check, grep invariants). Installing Playwright chromium — unprivileged, ~114 MB, with libasound.so.2 extracted from a .deb into a local prefix because apt install needs root — changed the CLASS of defect I could catch. Within one run it found: (1) trending_down MISSING from the subset icon font, rendering as the literal word TRENDING_DOWN at 44px in the hero badge, because my icon extractor matched a bare quoted x-text icon but not icons chosen inside a ternary; (2) NumberFlow exposes "value" as a GETTER ONLY, so assigning to it was a silent no-op — values go through update(); (3) optimalRegime bound in markup and defined nowhere, throwing on every render of the tax card; (4) setMarkers removed from the series object in Lightweight Charts v5. Every one of those is invisible to a parser and to grep. THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, which cost me two false failures: the harness's own assertions are code and can be wrong in exactly the way the app is. I reported "Tailwind not applied" because I read backgroundColor on a body whose gradient lives in background-image, and "hero shows no figure" because I scraped shadowRoot.textContent, which begins with the component's own style block. Both times the app was correct and my measurement was not. DIRECTIVE: when a check fails, establish whether the ARTEFACT or the PROBE is wrong before changing anything — and prefer asserting on structured state (a property, a bounding rect) over scraped text.

THREE DISTINCT MECHANISMS, none of them 'not trying hard enough': (1) I TEST THE DELTA, NOT THE STATE -- 94 modules carry real assertion-bearing smoke suites; I ran 9 in that session, the ones I had touched. There is NO TEST RUNNER in the repo (README says so outright), so 'run the tests' is not an operation anyone can perform, including me. (2) I WROTE FIXTURES FROM MY MENTAL MODEL OF THE DATA RATHER THAN FROM THE BYTES -- the transcript_timecode rule ended 'seconds?\\b' and never matched the real record, which reads '2 minutes 38 seconds2:38' with no word boundary; I wrote the test from the SHAPE of the record, tidied the join out, watched it pass, and reported the corpus clean while both transcripts sat in it. A green test over invented data is worse than no test. (3) NOTHING INSTRUMENTS RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN ARTIFACTS -- check_projections.py covers KB-to-projection only. The corpus pipeline is six artifacts (queue 1390 -> curation 580 -> engineer 2429 / personalization 862 -> blend 3291 -> pairs 444) and NOTHING reconciles any of them against any other. Every bug found that day lived in a RELATIONSHIP (queue-to-corpus duplication at 11 percent of the blend; conversations-to-pairs flattening; new-UI-surface-to-existing-metric blindness) and not one lived inside a module's own logic, which is exactly what unit smoke tests structurally cannot see. THE META-POINT THE USER WAS MAKING WITHOUT SAYING IT: every bug that day surfaced because they prompted me to look somewhere. None surfaced from systematic checking. So verification ran on THEIR attention -- the identical anti-pattern this entire repo exists to fight (the hearth exists because the heartbeat was borrowed from user attention; Antigravity's manual /memory produced zero records in months because it required remembering; relabel_domains went six days stale because nothing scheduled it). DIRECTIVE: 'I will verify more carefully' is a resolution and rots like every other resolution. The fix is an INSTRUMENT ON A CLOCK -- a runner that executes every suite, and cross-stage invariant checks over the pipeline -- so a regression reports itself unprompted instead of waiting for the user to ask the right question. Also: I raised THREE false alarms that same session (duplicate KB ids, transcripts back in the queue, assistant_summary reaching the corpus ungated), each from trusting a crude probe over reading the rows, which is the failure mode KB already has a directive about.

A METRIC ARGUED AGAINST A SPEND DECISION USING EVIDENCE IT DID NOT HAVE (2026-09-15). js-learning/stage_5_specialists/ROADMAP.md gates a Rs 1,480-2,960 RunPod training run on one question, and cites as urgency: '--ask has 19 sessions lifetime and 0 in the last 30 days -- training an adapter for a path nobody opens buys a better version of something unused.' THE NUMBER WAS AN ARTEFACT OF A BLIND PARSER. brain/usage.py::_session_times derived every session's time from the FILENAME. Terminal sessions are conv-20260911T155453-2960.jsonl and parse. The hearth's web UI writes conv-web-<uuid>.jsonl -- no timestamp in the name at all -- so every UI session hit a bare `continue` and vanished. Measured before the fix: last_session 2026-09-11, while the user was in that UI on the 14th and 15th answering a 45-question personalization set. After the fix (fall back to the first record's own `ts` inside the file): lifetime 21->23, recent 8->10, last_session 2026-09-14, days_since 1. WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A MISCOUNT: this module's whole reason for existing is that disuse was UNREPRESENTABLE -- its own header says 'every instrument here counts construction' and that conversations/ was the only usage signal with no consumer. It was built to make being-ignored visible, and then went blind to the surface the user actually adopted. A new UI shipped and nobody asked whether the usage metric could see it. SECOND-ORDER: the module's FLOW docstring said 'no file is opened, so this stays cheap enough for every boot' -- true when written, false the moment the fallback landed. Corrected in the same edit rather than left to rot, which is the thirteenth instance of prose-declares-X-code-does-not-X in this repo. DIRECTIVE: when a new surface, host or entry point ships, enumerate which EXISTING metrics can see it -- a measurement that silently excludes the thing being measured keeps reporting confidently. And when a roadmap cites a number as grounds for or against spending money, re-run the measurement before trusting the prose; the figure and the code that produced it drift independently.

TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY RUNNING THE LIVE PATH AFTER A MERGE, NEITHER VISIBLE TO ANY OFFLINE TEST (2026-09-15). After merging Antigravity's work I ran curate_turns against the real API rather than trusting the 38 passing offline tests. 3 of 3 turns came back 'UNPARSEABLE'. DEFECT 1 -- A MISLEADING ERROR MESSAGE, and it is mine: curate() caught EVERY exception and returned None, and run_backlog labelled every None 'UNPARSEABLE'. The actual cause was HTTP 402 -- the user's OpenRouter credits were nearly exhausted. A BILLING failure was being reported as a MODEL-QUALITY failure, which sends the next reader to tune the prompt when they should be topping up an account. Fixed by letting transport errors PROPAGATE from the organ so the adapter can tell the two apart: an unusable answer skips one turn, an unreachable model STOPS the batch (894 pending turns would otherwise each fail identically, costing real money to prove it). DEFECT 2 -- AN UNBOUNDED max_tokens, and a non-obvious interaction. The client never set max_tokens, so OpenRouter reserved the MODEL's maximum (65536) against the balance and refused: 'you requested up to 65536 tokens, but can only afford 62888'. The answer needed ~150. But capping it at 600 BROKE IT DIFFERENTLY -- the reply came back 64 characters, truncated mid-field at '"responds_to": "'. REASON, worth remembering: max_tokens bounds REASONING TOKENS AND VISIBLE OUTPUT TOGETHER, and the curator model reasons before answering, so the thinking consumed the whole budget. The cap must be sized for the answer PLUS however much the model thinks first; 4000 works and still reserves ~6% of an uncapped call. DIRECTIVE: after any merge that touches a network path, RUN THE LIVE PATH -- offline tests with an injected transport cannot see credit exhaustion, token ceilings, or reasoning-budget interactions, and all 38 curator tests passed while the feature was completely broken. DIRECTIVE 2: never collapse 'could not reach it' and 'it answered badly' into one error state. They have different causes, different fixes, and different correct responses (continue vs stop), and conflating them produces a confident message pointing at the wrong subsystem.

I REPEATED THE EXACT MISTAKE KB 589 RECORDS, THREE DAYS AFTER RECORDING IT (2026-09-14). On 2026-09-11 the user corrected me for addressing 'does Antigravity persist a readable transcript?' to CODEX -- I had reasoned from physical co-location (Codex runs on the same laptop and can inspect the filesystem) when the right basis was PRIVILEGED SELF-KNOWLEDGE (Antigravity knows its own state). I wrote that up as KB 589 and a directive. On 2026-09-14 I addressed q_004 -- 'build the Antigravity capture adapter' -- to Codex again, on the same reasoning, and the user again rerouted it: 'route q_004 also to antigravity'. WHY THE STORED DIRECTIVE DID NOT FIRE, which is the actually useful part: KB 589's directive was framed around ALIASES AND ROUTING KEYS -- 'when choosing a routing key, an addressee, or an alias, ask what about this is guaranteed to still be true in six months'. That framing is about the STABILITY of an attribute over time (model version, machine co-location), and it is correct but narrow. The 2026-09-14 case was not about stability at all: both Codex and Antigravity would still exist in six months. It was about WHOSE STATE THE TASK CONCERNS. The directive did not fire because I had recorded the instance's surface (volatile vs stable attributes) rather than its principle. THE PRINCIPLE, stated so it generalises: a task or question about X's own internals goes to X, regardless of who else is capable, better resourced, or physically closer. Capability and access are tie-breakers, never the first criterion. Antigravity could answer q_001 in one turn because it read its own files; Codex would have had to reverse-engineer them. SECOND-ORDER LESSON, and the reason this is filed as a Failure rather than a Cognitive_Pattern: a directive written from the SHAPE of one instance will not catch the next instance of the same principle wearing different clothes. When recording a correction, write the rule at the level of the principle and then note the instance as an example -- not the reverse. Check this against the other DIRECTIVE entries; several are phrased as the instance.

PROVENANCE BY CORPUS SELF-REFERENCE, not by a capture-time flag (2026-09-14, jarvis_core/agent/provenance.py). PROBLEM: text_hygiene.py can tell machine text from prose by form, but is blind to one class -- the user pasting ANOTHER AGENT'S REPLY back into the chat. That text is fluent first-person English with a plausible pronoun rate. Measured: a pasted Codex status report scored 2.26 first-person tokens per 500 chars while the weakest genuinely-good corpus row scored 1.24, so the contamination sat INSIDE the good range and no stylistic threshold could separate them. NEGATIVE RESULT THAT KILLED THE OBVIOUS FIX: a 'pasted: true' field set by the capture hook cannot be built. Claude Code does NOT record paste events -- pasted text is inlined into the user message exactly as if typed; grepping every transcript in ~/.claude/projects/ for paste markers returns nothing. The host does not know, so no hook reading the host can know. WHAT WORKS: when the user pastes an agent reply, that text is usually ALREADY in the corpus as an earlier turn's assistant_summary, because JARVIS captured it when it was produced. So provenance is recoverable by cross-referencing the capture stream against its own past: a user turn that repeats an EARLIER assistant turn was not composed now. Implementation is 8-word hashed shingles (word-level survives the reformatting a paste picks up, where substring matching does not) plus a streaming index. THREE PROPERTIES BEAT THE FLAG THAT CANNOT BE BUILT: it works RETROACTIVELY over all existing records where a new field would only describe future ones; it is HOST-INDEPENDENT because Codex and Antigravity turns land in the same queue; and it is grounded in a FACT (this text existed before) rather than a judgement about style. DIRECTION IS THE WHOLE MEASUREMENT -- scoring against ALL turns instead of EARLIER ones reports 100% echo for the user's own repeated --ask question, because the answer quotes the question back; six such records topped the first run and none was a paste. ECHO_CEILING=0.30 is the measured precision knee (2/2 above 0.30; 4/7 above 0.15, and the 0.15-0.30 band is a real phenomenon -- answering a numbered list point by point reuses the assistant's vocabulary). VALIDATION THAT MATTERS MOST: it caught a row my own hand-labelling had marked GOOD -- 2026-09-06T00:06, which says 'I edited section 7 of that file two hours ago and wrote KB 527'. The user did not do that; I did. My own text pasted back, invisible to the grammar gate AND to a careful human read, found only by the corpus cross-reference. GENERALISES: when a stylistic signal cannot separate two classes, look for a FACTUAL one in data you already hold, and check whether the host records the ground truth before designing around the assumption that it does.

UNTRACKED jarvis_data/chromadb/ (2026-09-11), REVERSING a decision recorded one day earlier. The prior line said 'chromadb/ stays tracked anyway -- a 22 MB regenerable index isn't worth committing OR worth ripping out mid-project.' That was defensible when written and was obsoleted by a NEW FACT, not by a better opinion: the hearth's scheduler runs reindex_memory on a 12-hour cadence and is intended to run on BOTH machines. chroma.sqlite3 is a 23 MB binary and .gitattributes marks *.sqlite3 binary, so it has NO merge driver -- two machines rewriting it on a clock produces an unresolvable binary conflict the first time both sides commit. merge=union rescues *.jsonl only. The trigger was the user asking 'can we turn the hearth on here and in antigravity and in codex too?' -- a question about topology that surfaced a latent data-integrity hazard nobody had connected to it. WHAT MADE THE REVERSAL SAFE, and the part that is the actual lesson: I TESTED the regeneration claim before removing 23 MB from version control, instead of trusting the sentence I myself had written the day before. Ran scripts/ingest.py against a real tracked PDF with JARVIS_ROOT pointed at a scratch directory -> 99 embeddings in 18.5s, so all 24 tracked PDFs rebuild in ~8 minutes; index_memory.py for jarvis_memory was already proven by repeated use. This mattered because the SAME claim about this SAME directory had already been wrong twice in opposite directions -- first 'research_papers is not regenerable because the PDFs are gitignored' (false, all 24 are tracked), then 'stays tracked anyway'. Two wrong claims about one directory, neither of which survived anyone actually running the command. DIRECTIVE: a decision may be reversed when a NEW FACT changes the calculus -- that is not churn, it is the system working -- but say WHICH fact changed and leave the prior reasoning visible rather than overwriting it, so the next reader can tell a reversal from a flip-flop. And before deleting or untracking anything on the grounds that it is 'regenerable', RUN THE REGENERATION COMMAND ONCE against a scratch target. A regeneration path that has never been executed is a hypothesis, not a backup.

SECOND UNDECLARED-DEPENDENCY FIND, AND THE FIRST ONE'S DIRECTIVE DID NOT PREVENT IT (2026-09-11). uvicorn and pydantic are imported DIRECTLY by JARVIS code -- serve/hearth.py::serve() does a hard 'import uvicorn'; agent/tool.py and agent/state.py import pydantic at MODULE level -- and NEITHER was in requirements.txt. Nothing had ever failed on this machine because both arrive as TRANSITIVE dependencies of chromadb, so the gap was invisible to every test, every run, and every self-test. CAUGHT ONLY BECAUSE THE DOCS CHANGED: NERVOUS_SYSTEM.md and AGENTS.md had just started instructing a NEW machine to run 'python3 scripts/hearth.py --background' as a first-run step. That instruction would have failed on a clean venv -- the newly-written migration guide contained a command that could not work on the machine it was written for. The audit that found it was 'grep every third-party import across scripts/ and jarvis_core, diff against requirements.txt', which takes seconds and had never been run. WHY THIS IS THE SECOND INSTANCE: bashlex (KB, 2026-09-10) was the same failure exactly one day earlier -- imported directly by agent/bash_classifier.py, undeclared, and its absence soft-failed the permission gate to ASK on every command. That entry's directive was written and did not generalize, because it was phrased as a fact about bashlex rather than as a check to run. CLASSIFICATION: a transitive dependency is a COINCIDENCE, not a contract. The package that supplies it can drop it in any minor release, and the failure then appears on a machine nobody was testing, in a code path the tests do not cover (serve() is not exercised by hearth's own smoke tests, which test the ASGI app object rather than binding). DIRECTIVE, phrased as an executable check rather than a fact: before shipping any setup instruction, and after adding any import, run the import-vs-requirements diff -- ast-parse every .py under scripts/ and jarvis_core, collect non-stdlib top-level module names, and diff against requirements.txt. Declare everything you import DIRECTLY even when something else already pulls it in. Genuinely optional imports stay undeclared but must be listed in a comment block saying so, or the next audit re-flags them as oversights.

A REDESIGN'S REGRESSION LIST MISSED A THIRD CONSTRUCTOR OF THE CHANGED CLASS (found 2026-09-10, during an unrelated Codex-migration regression sweep). The tension.py rewrite (commit 1c2aac9) changed Consolidator's contract: it now takes a detector= and derives insights from TensionFindings, not from engine.build_model().links (that path was deleted). The commit's own stated regression list was 'agent.correlation, agent.consolidator, agent.life_state_monitor, agent.capture, serve.scheduler, agent.react, orchestrator --final-boss' -- and consolidator.py's OWN self-test was correctly rewritten with a FakeDetector at the time. But mind.py ALSO constructs a bare Consolidator(engine=eng, append_fn=..., ...) inside its own Final-Boss-style fixture (build_consolidator(), C5/C7), with no detector= -- a SECOND, independent construction site the regression list never named and the diff never touched. Under the new (correct) design, no detector means zero insights, so C5 ('heartbeat-driven consolidation persisted learnings') and C7 ('writes are heartbeat-emitted') both silently started failing -- 13/15 instead of 15/15 -- and this went undetected for a full day because mind.py was never re-run after that commit. FIX: added a _StubDetector returning one real TensionFinding to mind.py's fixture, mirroring the FakeDetector already proven correct in consolidator.py's own tests. DIRECTIVE: when changing a class's constructor contract, grep the WHOLE repo for every construction site of that class -- 'grep -rn ClassName(' -- rather than trusting a regression list assembled from memory of 'the modules that use this.' A class's OWN test file is not guaranteed to be the only place that constructs it; Mind's Final Boss fixture built one independently and was never on anyone's list, including mine.

WROTE A REGEX TO APPROXIMATE A GRAMMAR WHEN I ALREADY HAD THE EXACT STRINGS QUOTED (found 2026-09-10, reconcile_codex_memory.py's placeholder filter). Needed to recognize Codex's own template placeholder sentences ('No durable user profile information has been observed yet.', etc.) so they are never mistaken for real memory content. I had ALREADY read and quoted all 5 real strings verbatim in this same file's own header comment -- then wrote a REGEX approximating their shared grammar instead of matching the strings themselves: 'no X (are|is)? (available|observed|recorded)? yet'. That regex missed 2 of the 5 known placeholders on its own first self-test run, because the real sentences use 'has been observed yet' / 'have been observed yet' -- a verb-phrase shape the regex's optional groups never accounted for, despite both exact sentences being quoted three lines above the regex that failed to match them. FIX: replaced the regex with a literal frozenset of the known strings (whitespace-normalized, lowercased), with the reasoning written down: the earlier lesson from today (KB 578/579, the SFT quality gate, capture.py's domain matcher) was 'an OPEN vocabulary cannot be safely matched by keywords.' This is the inverse case, and I mis-applied the same fix: here the vocabulary is NOT open, it is a SMALL, FIXED set of literal strings emitted by one specific piece of template code. When the space is genuinely enumerable, enumerate it exactly -- writing a generalized pattern for a closed set only introduces a NEW place for the pattern-vs-reality gap to reopen, and it did so immediately, on data I had already looked at directly. DIRECTIVE: before writing a regex to recognize known strings, ask whether the string set is actually closed. If it is, match the strings, not a hypothesized grammar for them -- and test the match against every real example already quoted in the same file before considering it done, not after.

A TEST THAT LOOKED ISOLATED SILENTLY READ AND ALMOST WROTE REAL PRODUCTION STATE (found 2026-09-10, building the Codex capture adapter's self-test). Four functions used the pattern 'def f(path: Path = MODULE_CONSTANT)' -- find_rollouts(root=SESSIONS_ROOT), load_thread_names(path=SESSION_INDEX_PATH), read_watermark(path=WATERMARK_PATH), advance_watermark(fname, ts, path=WATERMARK_PATH). THE BUG: a default ARGUMENT VALUE is evaluated ONCE, at function-definition time, and baked into the function object -- it is NOT looked up fresh from the module's globals on each call. So the test's 'import ingest_codex_sessions as mod; mod.SESSIONS_ROOT = tempdir; mod.WATERMARK_PATH = tempfile' had NO EFFECT on find_rollouts()/read_watermark()/advance_watermark() called with no explicit path argument -- they kept using the REAL ~/.codex/sessions/ and the REAL jarvis_data/.codex_ingest_watermark.jsonl, baked in when the module first executed. HOW IT WAS CAUGHT: the test asserted 'run() ingests 2 exchanges from the synthetic session' and got 0 -- because it was silently reading the REAL watermark, which (from an earlier real run in the same session) had already advanced past both real rollouts' timestamps, so every real exchange looked already-ingested. WHY IT WAS NOT WORSE: if that real watermark had NOT already covered everything, the same bug would have caused the 'offline' test to APPEND SYNTHETIC TEST DATA into the real observation_queue.jsonl and silently ADVANCE the real ingestion watermark -- a test corrupting production state while reporting green. Verified after the fact: queue stayed at 599 lines, watermark unchanged; no corruption occurred, but only by chance of ordering. FIX: changed every such signature to 'param: Optional[Path] = None' with 'param = Path(param) if param is not None else MODULE_CONSTANT' as the FIRST LINE OF THE BODY -- a plain name reference inside a function body IS looked up fresh from the module's globals on every call, unlike a default argument value. This preserves identical external behavior (call with no args -> real path) while making module-level monkeypatching in tests actually take effect. DIRECTIVE: never use a mutable module-level path/constant as a parameter's DEFAULT VALUE if that path might ever need to be swapped for testing -- resolve it inside the function body instead. Grep for 'def .*: Path = [A-Z_]+\)' across the repo's other adapters (capture.py, recall.py, tension.py) as a follow-up; none were audited for this specific pattern today.

WORKFLOW PROTOCOLS FIRE BY REQUEST-SHAPE, AND CARRY NO SELF-INVENTED DISCRETION LAYER ON TOP (fixed 2026-07-15; rescued 2026-09-10 from machine-local memory that had ZERO KB representation). CLAUDE.md's .agent/workflows/*.md protocols (dev.md, learn.md, architecture-review.md, etc.) previously triggered only on literal '/command' typing. Since dev work in this repo happens conversationally ('do it', 'build the guard'), the workflows never fired -- dev.md's Design Review verdict, Stress Test bullets, Debug Hooks section, and closing Memory-suggestion/Cognitive-scan rituals were silently skipped even while file-header/code-style conventions kept looking followed, creating an illusion of compliance. FIX: trigger is now request-SHAPE matched against each workflow's stated purpose, regardless of literal slash typing. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIX ITSELF: while drafting it, I proposed broadening the trigger AND adding a 'skip the full ritual for trivial asks' discretion layer on top. The user rejected only the added discretion, verbatim: 'there's a reason i made those.' Re-reading all 8 workflow files confirmed this was not pedantry -- every one independently ends with an IDENTICAL, VERBATIM 'MANDATORY COGNITIVE PATTERN SCAN (NON-NEGOTIABLE)' block, and 6 of 8 gate on a search_memory.py prior-art check as literal STEP 0. A deliberately consistent, repeated discipline across the whole system, not decoration. DIRECTIVE: once a workflow's own stated scope is met, run its actual content in full -- do not layer a second, self-invented judgment call about which pieces are 'worth it' for a given request. Generalizes beyond workflows: when the user has built an explicit structured process (a checklist, a protocol file, a gate), the correct response to 'is this too heavy for X' is to RAISE it explicitly and let the user recalibrate -- never to silently soften it.

SFT PAIRS BUILT: 440 (397 train + 43 held-out), and the measurement says the harder half is still unsolved (2026-09-10). scripts/build_sft_pairs.py transforms prose that was ALREADY question-shaped -- nothing authored, nothing fabricated. Engineer 359/400 (90%): DE lessons 142, SESSION_LEARNINGS bolded lessons 146, jarvis_core THE BIG PICTURE headers 71. Personalization 81/200 (40%): experience_map 23, kb_verbatim 12, literature 11, user_explanations 35. Every §8 criterion met but the counts -- source_path on all 440, messages format, stratified 10% held-out carved BEFORE training with a fixed seed, zero train/heldout leakage. THE HEADLINE, AND IT IS NOT THE GOOD NEWS: adding these pairs moves the personalization character share 13.4% -> 13.7%. Nothing. Because 90% of extractable pairs are Engineer by nature. So of the two failures the Antigravity review named, 'zero SFT pairs' is FIXED (now 5.7% of corpus chars) and the 87/13 ASYMMETRY IS NOT, and no further extraction will fix it -- the mechanical sources are Engineer-heavy by construction. THE FIX I REJECTED AND WHY: raising _PERSONALIZATION_REPEATS 1->3/4 (the review's Action 3) contradicts SFT_SPEC §7 and is internally inconsistent with the review's OWN Failure C, which warns that ~190K personalization tokens risks memorization -- repeating the same tokens 4x increases that risk rather than reducing it. Upsampling changes the ratio without adding information. THE ONLY REAL LEVER LEFT is more personalization SOURCE material (§6 decision-explanation sessions), which requires the user. DIRECTIVE: that is now the highest-value unblocked action in Stage 5 -- not more extraction, not more tooling.

MY ANTI-HALLUCINATION GUARD WAS DISCARDING 60% OF CORRECT VERDICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-10). The tension judge returns which prior a candidate clashes with; TensionJudge validates that the cited id was actually among the priors shown, so an invented reference cannot become a surfaced insight. Sound guard, but implemented as strict string equality. SYMPTOM: the ship-gate eval flapped -- the gold case passed at 0.95 twice, then failed at 0.00 on a later run, with everything else identical. I nearly wrote it off as model sampling noise. MEASURED INSTEAD by repeating the identical case 5 times: the judge found the contradiction ALL FIVE TIMES. On three of them it wrote the id as 'PRIOR 429' rather than '429' -- echoing the '[PRIOR 429]' label MY OWN PROMPT used to present the priors. Exact match rejected those as hallucinations, so a working detector looked 60% unreliable and its true-positive rate was silently cut by more than half. TWO FIXES, both needed: (1) the prompt now labels priors '[id=429]' and asks for the id 'exactly as it appears after id=, digits only'; (2) _match_prior normalises before comparing -- strips a leading PRIOR/KB/entry/id token, brackets and whitespace, then falls back to a digit extraction that only resolves when EXACTLY ONE prior matches. The guard is not weakened: an id never shown still resolves to None (asserted by T13f). Stability after the fix: gold positive 5/5, hard negative 3/3. THIRD INSTRUMENTATION LESSON IN TWO DAYS: ScanReport now counts 'discarded (uncitable prior)' SEPARATELY from 'judge said NONE', because conflating them is exactly how a 60% suppression rate hid inside a plausible-looking zero. DIRECTIVE: a validator that rejects malformed-but-correct output is a false-negative generator, and it fails silently by construction. When a guard drops something, COUNT the drops as their own category -- never fold them into the legitimate-negative bucket. And check whether your own prompt's formatting is what the model is echoing back.

A SECURITY-RELEVANT DEPENDENCY WAS UNDECLARED, AND ITS ABSENCE WAS INVISIBLE (found 2026-09-10 by a regression run). agent/bash_classifier.py parses shell commands into a bashlex AST to decide ALLOW vs ASK vs DENY for shell_run -- it is part of the shipped permission gate. was NOT in requirements.txt and was not installed anywhere on disk. WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the module soft-fails correctly (bash_classifier.py:174 -- ), so nothing broke, nothing warned, and no security hole opened. The ONLY symptom was ONE smoke test flipping (permgate 13/13 -> 12/13, 'T3 shell safe ALLOW' getting ASK). Everything else -- boot, the gate, --ask -- kept working while the classifier had silently degraded to 'ask about every command', which destroys exactly the precision it exists to provide. IMPORTANT CALIBRATION: this is a CAPABILITY loss, not a safety regression. The failure direction is conservative (ASK, never ALLOW), which is the correct design. But 'fails safe' is not the same as 'fails visibly', and a permission classifier that quietly stops classifying is a real defect. FIX: installed bashlex==0.18 and declared it in requirements.txt with the consequence written next to it. DIRECTIVE: when a component soft-fails on a missing optional import, the import MUST be declared as a hard dependency if the component is security-relevant -- and the degraded mode should announce itself, not merely be documented. Grep for across the safety layer and check each one is either declared or loudly reported.

ONE CLASSIFIER, TWO CONSUMERS, TWO MEANINGS OF THE SAME LABEL -- caught by the Final Boss (2026-09-09). Fixing the abstention conflation, I hard-coded domain_classifier.py's below-threshold fallback from 'general' to UNKNOWN. Correct for the ACTIVITY-domain consumer, where 'general' had no prototype and was pure abstention. But brain/router.py COMPOSES the same DomainClassifier with its own ROUTING prototypes, and there 'general' IS A REAL DESTINATION -- the general model pool, present in ROUTING_LABELS and mapped in _ROUTE_MAP. Abstaining in routing legitimately means 'send it to the general pool'. So my change made the router return a label outside its own vocabulary and the 50-query frozen gate fell below 80%: FINAL BOSS 7/8, leg 3 FAILED. Caught only because that harness exists and was re-run. FIX: fallback_label is now a per-consumer constructor argument (default UNKNOWN); the router passes fallback_label='general' with the reason written at the call site. Better than reverting -- it keeps the honesty fix where abstention really is abstention, and keeps the routing semantics where it is not. Final Boss restored 8/8. DIRECTIVE: before changing a SENTINEL VALUE in a shared component, enumerate the consumers and ask what that value MEANS to each one. A label can be an abstention in one caller and a legitimate category in another; the same string is not the same semantics. Grep for construction sites, not just for the constant.

A LONG QUERY RETRIEVES NEIGHBOURS, NOT THE THING IT CONTRADICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-09; this single fix was the difference between the detector finding nothing and working). The tension detector passed the WHOLE candidate entry as the retrieval query. Measured on the gold pair (KB 461 genuinely contradicts KB 429, confirmed by hand in KB 463): query = the full 1126-char entry -> 429 NOT IN THE TOP 15; query = its first 300 chars -> 429 at rank 9; query = one focused topic phrase -> 429 at rank 1, three times. CAUSE: a long entry covers several subjects, so its embedding is the AVERAGE of all of them and matches nothing sharply. It retrieves its own neighbours IN TIME (adjacent KB ids written the same day) rather than the specific decision it clashes with. Worse, the candidate's top TWO hits were ITSELF -- an entry is always its own strongest match, burning retrieval budget on a guaranteed non-prior. FIX: split the candidate into ~320-char overlapping windows (max 5), retrieve for each, union and dedupe; plus exclude the candidate's own entry_id explicitly rather than relying on the timestamp filter. RESULT: 461->429, 518->509 and 494->491 all now retrieve their true prior AT RANK 1, and the full pipeline (retrieval + judge, no hand-feeding) surfaces the 461/429 contradiction at 0.95 while staying silent on 518. WHAT THIS ALMOST HID: the first 30-day replay reported '0 findings'. The eval harness had passed 5/5 because I HAND-FED it the priors, so it measured the judge and not retrieval. DIRECTIVE: an eval that supplies its own inputs measures only the last stage. Instrument every stage of the funnel, and when a pipeline reports zero, prove WHICH stage produced the zero before believing it.

ABSTENTION HAD NO LABEL, AND THAT -- NOT THE SUBSTRING BUG -- WAS THE ROOT CAUSE (found + fixed 2026-09-09, on the user's insistence). The user rejected my proposed fix outright: 'I need a permanent solution, if we keep implementing better keyword matching it will result in the same bad labels that will silently kill the training corpus.' Correct, and investigating why produced a sharper diagnosis than I had. MEASURED ROOT CAUSE: guess_domain seeded best='general' and returned it on zero matches, so 'this turn is genuinely general' and 'I have no idea' were THE SAME TOKEN. Measured on the live queue: 309 of 583 records (53%) were labelled general, and ALL 309 had ZERO keyword hits -- not one was a positive classification. An abstention was literally unrepresentable, which is why 99 days and ~15% wrong labels went unnoticed. THE TRAP I ALMOST WALKED INTO: agent/domain_classifier.py, the embedding classifier built precisely BECAUSE keywords failed, ALSO fell back to 'general' below threshold. Swapping keywords for embeddings alone would have been more accurate and equally undiagnosable. THE FIX IS FOUR PROPERTIES, only the first about accuracy: (1) semantic not lexical; (2) UNKNOWN as a distinct outcome, never 'general' -- this converts an invisible failure into a counted one; (3) the cosine SCORE persisted next to every label so a wrong threshold is inspectable; (4) a 28-turn hand-labelled GOLD SET wired into check_projections.py, which already runs on the scheduler. Property 4 is what makes it permanent: any classifier drifts as the work moves, so the durable property is not being right today but SAYING WHEN IT STOPS BEING RIGHT. The gate proved itself immediately -- first run scored 68%, refused to pass, and its misses showed the prototypes had no seeds for AWS Glue, VACUUM, ADF, SFT or RunPod. Adding seeds for that real vocabulary: 89%. DIRECTIVE: any classifier that cannot say 'I do not know' will hide its own failure rate forever. Give abstention its own label before tuning anything else.

THE SURFACING DETECTOR WAS REPLACED, NOT TUNED (2026-09-09). agent/tension.py supersedes correlation.py's link-proposal path. WHY REPLACEMENT WAS THE ONLY OPTION, all three measured: (1) The old detector could only fire when a domain DECLINED (vol_drop <=> b_recent < 0.6*b_earlier). The numerator grows with every captured turn; the denominator is a frozen slice of history. So its ability to say ANYTHING decayed monotonically toward zero the more JARVIS was used -- ANTI-INDUCTIVE, the exact opposite of what a memory organ should be. Replaying the real queue: 75 turns -> 1 candidate, 115 turns -> 0, and _deterministic_confidence was never called even once, so the 0.60 floor rejected nothing. (2) Its output was never a memory: lifetime total three sentences, all 2026-06-18, all restating one volume shift. (3) Its 'confidence' was a hand-rolled weighted sum with a free 0.35 base capped at 0.70 -- every shipped insight read '70%' because that was the cap. WHAT REPLACED IT: candidate = what the user is doing now (KB appends AND verbatim observation_queue turns); corpus = their own 305 Decision/Failure/Cognitive_Pattern entries via the EXISTING chromadb index (no re-index -- entry_type/timestamp metadata was already there); output = a RELATION (REVERSES/REPEATS/RECONFUSES/NONE) against a NAMED prior, fail-closed to NONE on every error path. Reuses ContradictionJudge's discipline from brain/reasoning.py rather than inventing a second judge. DIRECTIVE: when a detector's gate becomes harder to satisfy as data accumulates, that is a design fault, not a tuning problem -- check the monotonicity of every threshold against volume before shipping it.

ROW 0b MEASURED AND IT IS NEGATIVE: THE FLOOR IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK (2026-09-08). The scheduler now runs the consolidator every 6h, and it ran three times today, each exiting ok. New life-state feed entries produced: ZERO. The feed still holds 3 insights, all from 2026-06-18, and life_state_monitor --peek still says '(nothing to surface)'. Measured cause via consolidate.py --dry-run: window=21d turns=115 domains=5 **links=0** floor=0.6. Compare the same command on 2026-09-06: 75 turns, 5 domains, 1 link at 0.592. So the corpus grew 75 -> 115 turns and the number of candidate links went 1 -> 0. TWO CONCLUSIONS, both load-bearing. (1) The 0.60 confidence floor is NOT the binding constraint. I had framed it as 'links cross the floor as the queue grows' and expected 0.592 to rise -- instead there is now nothing at ANY confidence. Lowering the floor would surface nothing, because CrossDomainCorrelationEngine finds no cross-domain relationship to score. (2) The plumbing was never the gate. Steps 2-7 fixed the pulse (a Stop hook, then a real clock), and the pulse is now demonstrably independent of the user opening --ask -- and the organ STILL has nothing to say. stage_6_integration/ROADMAP.md 6.10 already states the correct gate: 'ambient presence is worth exactly as much as the surfacing organ has to say... build 6.10 only after the organ demonstrably produces insights worth interrupting someone for -- measured, not assumed.' It is now measured. DIRECTIVE: before any further ambient/delivery work (step 8 Telegram push included), the open question is whether domain-volume correlation is the wrong detector for 'what did I forget', not whether the transport reaches the user. Building a push channel for an organ that emits nothing would be the most expensive way yet to learn this.

PYTHON GOTCHA that silently breaks log-grepping: on a str-mixin Enum, str(x) and f-string formatting DISAGREE. PermissionDecision is declared 'class PermissionDecision(str, Enum)' with DENY = 'deny'. Then: str(P.DENY) -> 'PermissionDecision.DENY' (Enum.__str__ wins), f'{P.DENY}' -> 'deny' (the str mixin supplies __format__, and f-strings call __format__ not __str__), repr(P.DENY) -> "<PermissionDecision.DENY: 'deny'>". Cost me a false test failure: the code logged the decision with an f-string ('deny') while the assertion searched for the str() form ('PermissionDecision.DENY'). The real hazard is not tests -- it is that a log line written one way and grepped the other NEVER matches, and a monitoring rule built on it silently never fires. DIRECTIVE: when logging an enum whose value must be machine-matched later, use repr() or .value explicitly, never bare interpolation. Fixed in Python 3.11+ for IntEnum via __str__ changes, but this repo runs 3.10 and the str-mixin case remains divergent regardless.

TWO DEFECTS IN THE SCHEDULER THAT BOTH LOOKED LIKE SUCCESS (2026-09-08, both caught by running it rather than testing it). (1) STAGGER SILENCED THE ONE-SHOT. Jobs carry initial_delay_seconds to avoid a thundering herd at daemon boot. hearth.py --tick-once builds a fresh Scheduler, so started_at is now, so EVERY job reported 'not due' -- the command printed 'ran: nothing was due' and did nothing, every time, while exiting 0. Fixed with tick(ignore_stagger=True); interval cadence still honoured so a one-shot cannot force a needless reindex. (2) A SHARED GUARD LET ONE JOB CLEAR ANOTHER'S. Both refresh_profile and reindex_memory guarded on the SAME command, scripts/check_projections.py, which exits non-zero if ANY projection is stale. Measured live: refresh_profile ran first, fixed the two projections it owns, and reindex_memory then saw exit 0 and recorded 'skipped -- guard reports nothing to do'. So the vector index would NEVER be rebuilt regardless of how far it drifted, and the skip counter would keep reporting healthy. Fixed by adding --only SUBSTRING to check_projections so each job guards on the artifact IT can fix. DIRECTIVE: a guard shared between two fixers is not a guard -- scope every conditional job to the exact artifact it repairs. And both of these are the DECORATIVE-CODE class again (tests pass, position makes it inert): the only way either surfaced was executing the real thing and reading what it actually did.

I SWITCHED A READER BEFORE MIGRATING ITS DATA, AND IMMEDIATELY BROKE THE GUARANTEE I WAS PROTECTING (2026-09-08, self-inflicted, caught within one command). Changing the life-state watermark from .surfaced_watermark (JSON) to .surfaced_watermark.jsonl (append-only log) was correct. But I edited the code first and left the new .jsonl EMPTY, so surfaced_ids() returned an empty set and the very next invocation re-surfaced insight 5b17b2bebd4e -- an insight already shown on 2026-06-18. That is exactly the 'NEVER NAG: each insight surfaces AT MOST ONCE, ever' guarantee the change existed to make durable. Nothing was lost (the feed was untouched and the re-surface reached me, not the user) and I folded the 3 legacy ids into the new log, which collapsed the accidental duplicate. DIRECTIVE: when relocating a store, the order is MIGRATE THE DATA, THEN SWITCH THE READER -- never the reverse. A reader pointed at an empty new location does not fail loudly; it reports 'nothing recorded yet', which is indistinguishable from a clean slate and silently voids every guarantee built on that record. Same shape as the index_memory tier-metadata bug (1030 chunks, 0 hits, looked like success).

THE TORN-LINE APPEND DEFECT: a flock does NOT make an append-only log safe (found 2026-09-08 by a test written for unrelated new code). A lock serialises concurrent writers. It does nothing about a writer that was KILLED mid-write, which leaves a final line with no newline terminator -- and the NEXT append then lands on that same line, so the torn record DESTROYS the good record appended after it rather than only itself. A fold over the log then loses both. Discovered because a smoke test wrote a corrupt watermark as '}{corrupt' with no trailing newline and the good event appended after it vanished; the assertion I expected to be trivially true failed. Audit result: kb_append.py has guarded this since it shipped ('Ensure we start on a fresh line even if the file lacked a trailing \n' -- seek SEEK_END, read the last byte, write \n if needed), and THREE other append-only logs had never copied it: agent/capture.py append_observation (the observation queue, written every single turn), agent/context_ledger.py archive_span (where a lost span makes an evicted context unrecoverable -- it defeats that module's entire purpose), and agent/life_state_monitor.py mark_surfaced. All three fixed; suites 18/18, 17/17, 20/20. DIRECTIVE: every append-only writer must heal a missing terminator BEFORE appending. The correct pattern already existed in this repo and three later call sites diverged from it -- when a subtle correctness guard exists in one place, grep for the other writers rather than assuming the idiom spread.

BOTH DEFERRED STEP-6 ITEMS RE-EXAMINED AND BOTH OF MY ORIGINAL RATIONALES WERE WRONG (2026-09-08). I had deferred content-addressed KB ids and the watermark event-fold with one sentence: 'both solve concurrent multi-writer conflicts that cannot exist until the hearth ships.' Measured before building: (1) CONTENT-ADDRESSED IDS -- the motivating L303 collision has NEVER OCCURRED. kb_append.py --audit over 558 entries with 258 explicit ids returns duplicate_ids {}. fcntl.flock plus single-user-at-a-time held for the file's whole life, and the hearth does NOT add a same-machine writer flock cannot serialise. So a risky rewrite of the widest-reach field in the repo (five consumers read id) would have prevented a failure with no instances. Replaced with a DETECTOR: projections.id_collisions() + a check_projections line. (2) WATERMARK -- mark_surfaced was ALREADY flock'd with a correct read-modify-write, so same-machine concurrency was never the hazard either. The real hazard was git: .surfaced_watermark was a TRACKED JSON object, and JSON has no union merge driver, so two laptops surfacing insights clobber each other's ids -- which breaks the never-nag guarantee this file exists to keep. Fix was smaller and better than an event-fold format: rename to .surfaced_watermark.jsonl and it inherits merge=union from .gitattributes for free. Concatenation IS merge. DIRECTIVE: 'defer until X exists' is only valid if X is VERIFIED to be the thing that creates the condition. I asserted the hearth would create the writers; flock already handled the same-machine case and git had already created the cross-machine case months earlier. Verify the precondition, not just the fix.

HEARTH v0 SHIPPED (2026-09-08, omnipresence step 7). jarvis_core/serve/hearth.py + scheduler.py: ONE always-on process owns the mutable state and the clock; every surface becomes a socket client. Raw ASGI, NOT FastAPI -- uvicorn 0.46 is already installed while fastapi/starlette are absent, so this adds ZERO dependencies, and a bare ASGI callable is testable with a fake receive/send pair with no socket at all (all 23 hearth tests run offline). Verified live: POST /v1/ask boots the real Mind, calls 4-9 tools, streams narration over SSE, and a SECOND request continued the same conversation session -- 'same mind' is now a routing property, not a sync problem. Safety posture is deliberately timid: binds 127.0.0.1 only AND re-checks the peer address per request, requires a bearer token even on loopback (loopback is not a boundary against other local processes), serialises to one request at a time with 409 rather than interleaving mutable session state, and DENIES every permission prompt while reporting the denial in the response. DIRECTIVE: --ask keeps its in-process default and gains opt-in --via-hearth, because the hearth has no TTY so it cannot honour a human gate -- routing the terminal there by default would SILENTLY REDUCE capability. That flips to default once the Commitment gate (step 10) provides remote approval.

STEP 6 NARROWED, AND TWO OF ITS THREE PARTS WERE PREMATURE (2026-09-08). Investigating step 6 produced three findings that shrank it, and I reported rather than executed the original scope. FINDING 1 -- I HAD MY OWN DIAGNOSIS WRONG. I called the 544-vs-533 gap 'the mind disagrees with itself'. It was real but it SELF-HEALS: profile_synth.py rebuilds the index whenever it runs, and all three artifacts now read 557. It was never a fork, it was a STALENESS WINDOW that opens on every KB append and closes on the next regeneration. So the defect was never that projections go wrong -- it is that NOTHING LOOKS. I found it by accident, and accident is not a detection strategy. FINDING 2 -- parts 1 and 3 fix a conflict that cannot occur yet. Content-addressing KB ids fixes the L303 collision (kb_append._next_id is max(ids,300)+1, so two machines mint the same id) and the watermark event-fold buys multi-device merge safety. But CLAUDE.md:58 states the operating model: 'Single-user-at-a-time -- no concurrent edits.' Concurrent writers do not exist until the hearth does (step 7), and part 1 has the widest blast radius in the repo -- search_memory, kb_compact, cognitive_index, profile_synth and the new index_memory all read id. Deferred to step 7, where the writers actually appear. FINDING 3, AND IT CHANGED THE DESIGN RATHER THAN THE TIMING -- 'demote projections out of git' WOULD HAVE BROKEN THE PERSONAL LAPTOP. cognitive_profile.md and activity_digest.md are projections AND ALSO THE SYNC TRANSPORT: js-workspace-rule.md:21-22 tells that machine to READ both at boot, and line 25 records why it cannot rebuild them -- 'there is NO per-prompt capture here (Antigravity has no hook system)'. No local queue means no digest. Untracking them looks like obvious cleanup and blinds the other machine. So KB 548's taxonomy gains a third class: FACT (authoritative, tracked) / PROJECTION (derived, rebuildable WHERE READ, untracked) / PROJECTION-AS-TRANSPORT (derived here, consumed by a machine that CANNOT rebuild it, tracked and correctly so). ALSO VERIFIED FALSE: CLAUDE.md:123 claimed ChromaDB 'never committed' and pointed at scripts/sync_chromadb.py for regeneration. ChromaDB IS committed (17 files, 19MB) and that script DOES NOT EXIST -- wrong on both counts, the sixth prose-vs-code instance this week. And untracking chromadb is unsafe: research_papers' 156 embeddings cannot be regenerated because the source PDFs are gitignored too. SHIPPED: jarvis_core/brain/projections.py (14/14) as the core organ -- I first wrote the logic in scripts/ and corrected it, since this repo's contract is core organ + thin adapter; scripts/check_projections.py is now the CLI, exit 1 on stale so it works from a hook or CI rather than only for a human who remembered to look. Registered as a boot-inhale provider that returns None when healthy, so a clean system costs ZERO prompt tokens and only a real problem speaks. Untracked cognitive_index.sqlite3 and behavioral_state_model.jsonl; asserted the transport artifacts are still tracked, because that is the plausible-looking mistake. PROVEN: appended a KB entry without regenerating -> both zero-tolerance projections reported STALE at (-1) with the fix command and exit 1; ran profile_synth -> green, exit 0. STEP 5 SHIPPED: MEMORY NOW ARRIVES UNPROMPTED — the moat mechanism works for the first time (2026-09-08). MemoryManager (928 lines, 51 tests) had ZERO production construction sites, so react.py's auto-retrieve branch was unreachable on every real --ask and memory reached the prompt ONLY when the model chose to call a tool. That is verbatim ENDGAME Sec1.2's failure: 'it cannot fire when you did not know to ask.' TWO PREREQUISITES HAD TO LAND FIRST AND I NEARLY SHIPPED WITHOUT EITHER. (1) THERE WAS NOTHING TO RETRIEVE. Measured: ChromaDB held exactly ONE collection, research_papers, 156 embeddings. The knowledge base, conversations and observation queue were NOT indexed at all. Wiring auto_retrieve_top_k>0 that day would have auto-retrieved RESEARCH PAPERS and LOOKED LIKE THE FEATURE WORKED — the most dangerous possible outcome. This is boot.py's own founding L324 bug still live: 'asked what have we built, searched one ChromaDB collection of research papers and honestly found nothing, while knowledge_base.jsonl sat unread.' The 2026 fix then was prior_self_consult as a TOOL, which is exactly why memory required asking. Built scripts/index_memory.py: streams the KB, renders type+tags+content so a hit carries provenance, chunks via the existing RecursiveWordChunker (900/180, respecting MiniLM's 256-token ceiling per KB 508), upserts by deterministic id into a new jarvis_memory collection. (2) A SECOND, INVISIBLE PREREQUISITE: metadata.tier. MemoryManager.retrieve queries with where={'tier': tier.value}, so records lacking that field are invisible. 1030 correctly-indexed chunks returned ZERO hits until tagged tier='warm'. WARM is right, not HOT — HOT is an in-process LRU that dies with the process; the KB is durable and semantically searchable. A THIRD BUG FOUND BY DISBELIEVING A PLAUSIBLE NUMBER: the first dry-run reported 254 entries against a 554-line KB. Cause: the KB has TWO SCHEMA GENERATIONS — 250 entries carry uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) (plus source_machine), 281 older ones carry only content/expiry/tags/timestamp/type. Keying on uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) silently skipped 300 entries, 54% of the mind's memory, and '254' was plausible enough to pass. Fixed with stable_key(): uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) when present, else a content hash — now 554 entries / 1030 chunks. Same silent-partial-coverage class as KB 508. VERIFIED, and the isolation matters: with ZERO tools available so nothing COULD be asked for, the assembled system prompt already contained 'tier=WARM score=0.05 id=kb-538-1' verbatim including the exact constant _DEFAULT_BUDGET_USD. Memory arrives BEFORE the model gets a turn. Wired in boot.py only when a store is open (no store -> no WARM tier -> auto-retrieve would burn a query per turn for nothing); _AUTO_RETRIEVE_TOP_K=4 because every item is a standing per-turn token tax, not a one-off. Regression: memory_manager 51/51, react 112/112, mind 15/15, boot 20/20, permgate 13/13, compact 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. HONEST CAVEAT ON ROW 0b: a live --ask still ALSO called prior_self_consult, so the strict acceptance test ('no memory tool in the call list') did not pass — the model has a tool it likes and will keep using it. What is proven is that the unprompted channel now works and reaches the prompt first. Whether it makes JARVIS say the thing you did not ask for is the measurement that remains, and index_memory.py must be RE-RUN as the KB grows or retrieval silently goes stale.
